habitat: Grassy clearings and short grass in mesic and semi-arid savanna, especially beside bushwillow or mopane, and also heavily grazed paddocks and gravel roads.
summary: A non-breeding intra-African migrant to the lowveld. It is dark above, with bold markings on the face and breast, a heavier bill than a Groundscraper Thrush, and white legs. It flicks its wings open while walking and flies with a sharp dip. The sexes are not described as differing. Newman states that it has no distinctive call. Juvenile and chick colours are not described.

similar.note: Groundscraper Thrush has similar bold face and breast markings. Dusky Lark is darker above, with a more robust bill and white legs, and it flicks the wings while walking.
Rufous-naped Lark is a resident with rufous wings and a whistled song. Dusky Lark is a dark migrant of clearings and does not have that song.

viewNotes.note: Dark upperparts. The flight is sharply dipping. A separate upperwing pattern is not described.
The underwing is not described. It flicks the wings open while walking, which is not a spread-wing flight view.
Bold face and breast markings. The bill is robust and the legs are white.
Dark upperparts, darker than a Groundscraper Thrush. The rump is not given a separate colour in the texts used here, though an old name is rufous-rumped bush lark.
Dark upperparts, bold face and breast pattern, heavy bill and white legs, usually on open ground in woodland.

calls.description: Newman states that it has no distinctive call. The texts used here do not transcribe a song or assign any sound to one sex.

research.note: Status is intra-african-migrant, matching Kemp’s non-breeding visitor. SABAP1 and Roberts say it arrives from late October into November and returns north from April to June, so months are October–June. The two xeno-canto recordings found were both ND and were not used. Breast and face colours are described only as bold and dark, not as a named palette beyond that. Chick and juvenile plumage are not described. An old English name, rufous-rumped bush lark, is recorded by Wikipedia without a plumage description in the texts used here.
